true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Immediate-delete path cancels in SendGrid but leaves the reminder row marked as scheduled

When `immediateDelete` is true and a referenceId exists, the function cancels the batch in SendGrid and returns without touching the `workflowReminder` row. The row keeps `scheduled: true` and its referenceId, and `cancelled` stays null. The cron job never picks it up for cancellation because it only selects `cancelled: true` rows, so the row lingers until its scheduledDate passes. This affects the reschedule path in handleNewBooking.ts, which passes `true`, and it is inconsistent with the cancel path, which sets the flag and expects the row to be removed later. The behaviour across the immediate and deferred modes should be made consistent.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.

The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancellation of reminders due within the next hour is deferred and can still send

For a cancelled booking, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` is called without `immediateDelete`, so it only sets `cancelled = true`. The actual SendGrid cancel happens in the cron job, which runs every 15 minutes and only picks up reminders whose `scheduledDate` is within the next hour. If a booking is cancelled 5 minutes before a reminder is due, and the cron last ran before the cancellation, the email can be sent before the next cron run actually cancels it. The same deferred path is used by the reschedule flow in bookings.tsx. Reminders whose `scheduledDate` is inside the cron window at cancellation time should be cancelled immediately in SendGrid, and only the rest should be deferred.

No tests cover the new cancelled-reminder semantics or the cron cancellation path

The PR changes the cancellation model (new `cancelled` column, deferred cancellation in the cron job, immediate vs deferred in `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`), but no tests were added. Neither the cron cancellation loop, including its failure handling, nor the branching in `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` is covered. Those are exactly the paths where the reported bugs occur, so the regressions described above would not be caught.

One failing SendGrid cancel aborts the whole cancellation batch and blocks it on every run

The loop at lines 56-73 awaits `client.request` for each cancelled reminder inside a single try block. If the request throws for one reminder (for example SendGrid rejects a batch that was already sent or no longer exists), the exception skips every remaining reminder in `remindersToCancel`, and the catch only logs. Those reminders keep `cancelled: true` and are never cancelled or deleted. The query always returns the same ordered set, so the failing reminder is hit first again on the next 15-minute run and the rest stay stuck indefinitely. One bad row can therefore stop all cancellations, which is the same failure mode this PR is meant to fix. Each reminder should be cancelled in its own try/catch so that failures are isolated and the row is retried or logged individually.

Paid booking cancellation returns before workflow reminders are cancelled

The `if (bookingToDelete.paid)` branch refunds the payment, marks the booking REJECTED and returns early at line ~464. The reminder cancellation block (`updatedBookings.forEach(... deleteScheduledEmailReminder / deleteScheduledSMSReminder)`) is placed after this return, so workflow reminders of paid bookings are never cancelled. Customers of paid, cancelled bookings still receive workflow reminders, which is the bug this PR claims to fix.

SMS cancellation has no retry and the DB row is only removed if Twilio cancel succeeds

In `deleteScheduledSMSReminder`, if `twilio.cancelSMS` throws, the function jumps to the catch and the reminder row is not deleted. Nothing retries the cancellation, unlike the email path, which at least has a cron. A transient Twilio error therefore lets the scheduled SMS for a cancelled or rescheduled booking go out. The same failure mode this PR fixes for email remains for SMS.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Making the forEach callback async moves getCalendar errors out of the try/catch

Before this change, `getCalendar` was synchronous, so a throw inside it was caught by the surrounding try/catch and logged. Now the callback is async and the `await getCalendar(...)` and `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` promises are not awaited by `forEach`, so rejections become unhandled promise rejections and the try/catch never sees them. The cancellation work also runs fire-and-forget, so the reschedule returns before calendar/video deletion finishes. The same pattern is in packages/app-store/wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

false_positives.candidate:
Adapter creation is now sequential and awaits each app in a loop

`getVideoAdapters` used to build adapters synchronously in one pass. It now awaits each app import one at a time in a `for` loop, so N credentials cost N sequential module-load round trips. Resolving the apps with `Promise.all` would preserve ordering and avoid the serialized waits.

Async forEach pushes into apiDeletes after it has already been awaited

Inside the recurring-cancellation branch, `.forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })` pushes to `apiDeletes` only after an asynchronous await. `forEach` does not wait for these callbacks, so `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` runs before the pushes happen. Those deletions are never awaited, their errors are unhandled, and the response can report success while calendar events are still being deleted. Replace the forEach with a for...of loop or `Promise.all` over the credentials.

getCalendarCredentials stores un-awaited getCalendar promises as the calendar value

`getCalendarCredentials` is still synchronous, but `getCalendar` now returns a Promise, so `calendar` is a Promise on every returned item. Any consumer that checks `if (!calendar)` or uses the value as a Calendar synchronously will be wrong. A rejected `getCalendar` promise (for example from a failing CalendarService constructor) is also only handled when `getConnectedCalendars` later awaits it, so the rejection can be reported late or unhandled. The function should be made async and should await the calendar, or the field type should be updated to match.

import() calls run eagerly at module load, so nothing is actually lazy

Each entry is `import("./x")` evaluated when the object literal is created, so every app module starts loading as soon as `appStore` is imported, regardless of whether it is used. The async wrapping therefore adds no lazy-loading benefit on the server or in client bundles. Entries should be thunks (`() => import("./x")`) and callers should invoke them on demand. Any rejected import is also created up front, so a broken app module can surface as an unhandled rejection even if nothing ever awaits it.

requestReschedule fires async calendar/video deletions without awaiting them

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...)` discards the promises returned by each callback. The mutation then sends the reschedule email and returns while the `getCalendar` lookup and the `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` calls are still running. Any rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection, and the client cannot know whether the old calendar event was actually removed. Use `Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` and await it.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check uses the slot start for both start and end

`end` is computed from `slotStartTime` instead of the slot end time, so `end > workingHour.endTime` is effectively checking the start again. A slot that runs past the end of working hours is not rejected. Also, `workingHours.find` returns true when any single working-hours block excludes the slot, so a slot inside a later block (e.g. 14:00-18:00 when there is also a 09:00-12:00 block) is rejected. The check should ask whether the slot fits inside at least one block (`.some` with start >= startTime and end <= endTime).

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Date-override end check compares Dayjs objects by identity

`dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` compares two freshly created Dayjs object references, so it is always false and the zero-length override branch never triggers. It should use `.isSame(...)`. As written, a zero-length override (start equals end) is not handled as intended.

false_positives.candidate:
New timezone test would pass without the fix

The added assertion uses the +6:00 timezone and expects the same UTC slots (08:30-11:30Z) as the +5:30 case. Slot times are returned as UTC ISO strings, so this output is independent of the invitee timezone, and the old `getUTCHours` code would produce the same result. The test does not check that a date override adapts to a different timezone. There is also no test for the main fix: a round-robin event where a fixed host's date override must respect that host's busy times.

Override timezone may be undefined, falling back to server timezone

`dayjs(...).tz(override.timeZone)` is called without guaranteeing `override.timeZone` is set. The timeZone is copied from `availability.timeZone` in slots.ts, which may be missing. dayjs `.tz(undefined)` then uses the process's local timezone, so the computed offset depends on the server's TZ setting rather than the organizer's. The overrides' timezone should be validated or defaulted to the organizer timezone.

Slot inside a date override skips the busy-time check entirely

When a date override exists for the slot's day and the slot falls inside it, `checkIfIsAvailable` returns true right away (`if (dateOverrideExist) return true;`). That bypasses the `busy` check at the end of the function. A fixed host with a date override who already has a calendar event or booking at that time will still be reported as available. This is the exact problem the PR is meant to fix (round-robin events booked while fixed hosts are unavailable), so the fix is incomplete.

Brittle hard-coded responses.calls index

The assertion changed from `responses.calls[0]` to `responses.calls[2]` to check the JWT header. This depends on the exact ordering of mocked HTTP calls, including the new OAuth calls. true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.

false_positives.candidate:
Closing one strategy shuts down the factory's shared queue pool, so later assignments silently drop messages

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` (and `terminate()`/`join()`) call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. The pool is owned by the factory (`ResultsStrategyFactory.queue_pool`) and is reused by every strategy that `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` builds. When StreamProcessor closes a strategy on a rebalance and then calls `create_with_partitions` again, the new strategy gets a pool whose workers have been told to stop and whose queues are shut down. In `submit()` the `put()` on a shut-down queue raises, the broad `except Exception` marks the offset complete via `offset_tracker.add_offset`/`complete_offset`, and the offset is then committed. The message is never processed and never redelivered. The pool should be owned and shut down only by the factory, not by a strategy that merely borrows it.

Offsets are committed from the background commit thread, outside the consumer's processing thread

`_commit_loop` runs on its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which invokes the arroyo `Commit` callable obtained in `create_with_partitions`. Arroyo's consumer and its `Commit` are designed to be driven from the StreamProcessor thread, which also calls `poll()`/`consumer.commit`. Calling commit concurrently from a second thread is not safe for the underlying consumer and can race with rebalance handling and poll. The commit should be marshalled back to the processing thread (for example in `poll()`), or the thread-safety of the consumer path should be explicitly established.

Processing failures are logged and then committed, so the message is silently lost

In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, any exception from `result_processor` is logged and the `finally` block marks the offset complete. The commit loop then advances past it, so the failed item is never retried and never reprocessed. The class and module docstrings state 'No item is lost' and 'Only commits offsets after successful processing', which is not what the code does. This should either be documented as at-most-once for failures or the failure should block or retry the commit.

Queues are unbounded, so the claimed backpressure never happens

`FixedQueuePool.__init__` creates `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `submit()` uses a plain `put()`. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`'s docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but nothing ever fills up. If workers are slower than Kafka delivers, the in-memory backlog grows without bound and the consumer never pauses. `poll()` only emits a gauge.

Worker shutdown relies on queue.Queue.shutdown(), which only exists on Python 3.13+

`queue.ShutDown` and `Queue.shutdown()` were added in Python 3.13. On older interpreters `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` raises AttributeError, which is caught and only logged in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()`. Workers stay blocked in `work_queue.get()` forever. `shutdown()` then waits up to 5 seconds per worker (`worker.join(timeout=5.0)`) for up to 20 workers, blocking close for about 100 seconds. The version requirement should be verified, or a sentinel-based shutdown used instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Folder tree stays cached for 30s after folder creation, so inherited access to new nested folders is denied

buildFolderTree caches the namespace folder tree for shortCacheTTL and nothing invalidates it on folder creation. The fallback to the DB only refreshes permissions, not the folder tree. For a folder created within the TTL, e.g. grandchild C under a newly created child B under a folder A the user already has access to, the tree lacks C (and possibly B). checkInheritedPermissions then calls tree.Ancestors(C), which cannot reach A, so the creator is denied on a dashboard in C even though they hold a grant on A. This is the same user-facing bug the PR aims to fix, and it is not covered by the new fallback. Refresh the folder tree on a miss for the requested folder, or invalidate it on folder creation.

New cache tests do not cover the behaviour the PR is meant to fix

TestService_CacheCheck covers cache hits, DB fallback on a miss or outdated map, and a pre-set explicit denial. It never checks that a DB denial populates the denial cache, nor that a permission granted after a denial is honoured (the creator scenario). It also has no test for inherited access through a folder created after the tree was cached, and no test for denial key collisions. These are the scenarios that would catch the staleness and key issues above.

Permission denials are cached for 30s with no invalidation, so a newly granted permission stays denied

When the DB check returns not-allowed, the result is stored in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL (30s), keyed by user, action, name and parent folder. Nothing invalidates this entry when permissions change. The PR's stated goal is that a creator can access a dashboard or folder they just created. If the user is first denied on that name (for example a fetch before creation), the denial is then served from cache for up to 30s even though the DB now grants access. The denial cache check at line 116-121 returns before the DB fallback runs, so the new-permission fallback never applies during that window. Either skip caching denials, use a much shorter TTL, or invalidate the entry when a permission or resource is created.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete success metric uses the object name in the kind label position

recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) passes `name` where the other calls pass options.Kind. The kind label of the metric is therefore set to the object name, creating unbounded label cardinality and making the metric inconsistent with the other methods.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy Update reuses objInfo that the storage Update has already consumed

objInfo is passed to d.Storage.Update (line 126) and then reused in the legacy goroutine (line 139). UpdatedObjectInfo.UpdatedObject is typically called once per store and may consume or mutate the old object; calling it concurrently from the goroutine races with the storage path. Also the legacy update may compute its update from a different base object than the one storage used, so the two stores can diverge without any error being surfaced.

Async legacy writes run on the request context, so they are cancelled once the request returns

Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection launch the legacy write in a goroutine using a context derived from the request ctx (e.g. line 51 `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). The HTTP request context is cancelled when the handler returns, which happens right after the storage write succeeds. The legacy write will therefore often fail with context canceled, and the failure is only recorded in metrics. Legacy writes can silently be skipped, which defeats the purpose of mode 3's safety copy. The goroutine should use a detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx)) plus the timeout.

Error test for Create passes only because the legacy expectation matches the storage call

The 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' case registers no storage expectation (setupStorageFn is nil). The storage Create call therefore matches the legacy mock expectation at line 41 and returns the error by accident. The test does not check what it claims to check, and a change in the call pattern would make it panic instead of asserting.

Get test creates its own registry while the other tests share the package-level registry

TestMode3_Get creates a new prometheus registry (line 119) while all other tests, and the mode1 test after this change, use the shared package-level `p`. Mixing the two patterns is inconsistent and makes it unclear whether the dual writer metrics are registered more than once on the shared registry across subtests.

Legacy write failures in async goroutines are not logged

Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection run the legacy write in a goroutine and only record a metric on error. There is no log call, so a failed legacy write leaves no trace in logs and divergence between the stores is invisible to operators. The old code logged these failures, so this is a regression in observability.

Mode 3 playlist integration tests check legacy consistency immediately after writes that are now asynchronous

doPlaylistTests asserts legacy API results right after k8s creates, updates and deletes (for example the legacy list check after Create, and getFromBothAPIs after Update). With mode 3 the legacy write runs in a background goroutine, so these checks can race with it and fail intermittently. The new mode 3 subtests need a wait or retry before comparing the legacy store, or the assertions must be relaxed for mode 3.

Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy write or wait for it

The tests set legacy mock expectations but never assert they were called (AssertExpectations is not used), and the goroutines are not awaited. Tests pass even when legacy is never written, and goroutines can call mocks after the test has finished. The behavior that defines mode 3 (legacy write happens and does not fail the request) is not tested.

Object passed to the async legacy Create is shared with the storage Create and may be mutated concurrently

The same `obj` is handed to d.Storage.Create (line 42) and then to d.Legacy.Create inside a goroutine (line 55). Storage create implementations typically mutate the object (set ResourceVersion, UID, creationTimestamp, name generation). The legacy goroutine therefore reads an object that may be written concurrently or is already modified, which is a data race and can write inconsistent data to legacy. The legacy path should get a DeepCopy taken before the goroutine starts, or the storage result should be used.

Storage Update failure is recorded as a legacy duration metric

In the Update error path, the failure is recorded with d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) and startStorage, even though the failing call was the storage write. This corrupts legacy metrics and hides storage failures from the storage metric.

Unrelated module checksum entries added to go.work.sum

The go.work.sum diff adds checksums for unrelated modules (grafana-azure-sdk-go/v2, prometheus-alertmanager, otel exporters, genproto rpc, etc.) that have nothing to do with the dual writer change. These look like incidental tooling output and should be removed from this PR to keep the change focused.

Update goroutine creates its timeout context before startLegacy and without a defer on the same line

In the Update goroutine (lines 135-138) the timeout context is created before the timer starts and the cancel is deferred after an unrelated statement. This is harmless today but is inconsistent with the other goroutines and makes the cancel easy to miss if the function is edited. Low priority.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Write lock taken without re-checking the cache, and held across file and CDN I/O

The fast path reads the cache under RLock, releases it, then takes the write lock at line 48 without checking the cache again. Every goroutine that misses the cache during startup, or after a failed load, will queue on the write lock and each one re-runs the manifest read and, when configured, the HTTP fetch to the CDN. The lock is held for the whole rebuild (lines 48-70), including the network call in readWebAssetsFromCDN, which has no timeout beyond the request context. Before this change, readers never blocked. Now every request that reaches GetWebAssets blocks on the write lock for as long as a slow CDN takes to respond. Fix: after acquiring the write lock, re-read entryPointAssetsCache and return it if it is now non-nil and not in Dev mode. Consider doing the I/O outside the lock and taking the lock only to publish the result.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error path caches nil and returns a stale-looking result

On error, result is nil and line 69 overwrites the global cache with nil, so the cache is cleared even if a previous good value existed (for example, in Dev mode where the cache is reloaded on every call). The function then returns nil with err. Callers that ignore err will get a nil pointer. This behaviour is unchanged by the diff, but the new locking makes it more visible: a transient read failure during a Dev reload now clears the shared cache for concurrent readers. Consider only assigning the cache when err == nil.

false_positives.candidate:
No test covers the concurrent access this change is meant to fix

The PR fixes a data race on entryPointAssetsCache, but no test is added or changed. A test that calls GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines, ideally under go test -race and covering both Dev and non-Dev environments, would show the race is fixed and would catch the locking regression described above.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false, making the feature-flag check meaningless

The helper reads the FlagSqlExpressions toggle, negates it, and then returns false on both branches, so it is hard-coded to false regardless of the flag. The flag check at the call site in ReadQuery therefore never does anything useful. The disable is intended, but the code reads as if it honours the flag. Anyone who later edits one branch could unintentionally re-enable SQL expressions. The helper should be replaced with an explicit unconditional rejection, with a comment stating that SQL expressions are disabled for the security fix.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

false_positives.candidate:
No test covers the new SQL-disabled rejection path

The PR changes ReadQuery so that QueryTypeSQL always returns 'sqlExpressions is not implemented', but no test was added or updated to assert this. Without a test, a future change that re-enables the path (for example by fixing enableSqlExpressions) would not be caught. A regression test should assert that a SQL query is rejected with and without the feature flag enabled.

NoData result is unconditionally overwritten by TableData

When frame.Rows() == 0, rsp.Values is set to NoData, but the next statement unconditionally reassigns rsp.Values to TableData. The NoData branch is dead code, so empty SQL results are always returned as TableData. This is pre-existing and not introduced by the PR, but it sits in the same Execute function being edited here and should be fixed (for example with an else).

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Finer locking lets concurrent builds for the same key race and overwrite each other

Removing the function-wide lock means two `BuildIndex` calls for the same NamespacedResource can run at once. This can happen when `getOrCreateIndex` builds on a Search request while `search.init` is still building the same key, or when a watch event triggers a build. Both paths call `bleve.New` on the same directory for file-backed indexes, and the second call fails. For in-memory indexes, the second build silently replaces the cache entry, leaking the first index and any writes made to it. Nothing in `getOrCreateIndex` or `BuildIndex` deduplicates builds per key, and the TODO in `getOrCreateIndex` acknowledges this. A per-key singleflight or lock is needed before this change is safe.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the cache map without holding cacheMu

`TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` with no lock, while `BuildIndex` writes to the same map under `cacheMu.Lock()`. The commit removed the whole-function lock and only leaves the map write protected, so this read is now clearly unsynchronized. Concurrent `BuildIndex` calls (for example from `search.init` or a watch-triggered `getOrCreateIndex`) can cause a 'concurrent map read and map write' fatal error. `TotalDocs` should take `cacheMu.RLock()`.

false_positives.candidate:
Context cancel function is leaked when startup Init fails

`ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` is created earlier in `NewResourceServer`. When `s.Init(ctx)` fails, the function returns `nil, err` without calling `s.cancel()`, and any goroutines started by the lifecycle hook or by `initWatcher`/`search.init` keep running with no owner. The error path should call `cancel()`.

Data race on shared `err` and counter in parallel index build goroutines

Inside `init`, each `group.Go` closure runs concurrently and does `totalBatchesIndexed++` (line 189) and `_, _, err = s.build(...)` (line 190). Both `totalBatchesIndexed` and the outer `err` are shared across goroutines, so this is a data race. A failing build can also overwrite another goroutine's error, so `group.Wait()`'s result may not reflect the real failure. The fix is to use a local `err` inside the closure and an atomic counter. This matters more now because the index is built synchronously in the constructor and the locking was made finer, so more builds run concurrently.

Events written during the index build are never indexed

`init` lists resources and builds the index first, and only afterwards calls `WatchWriteEvents`. The SQL backend's poller starts from the latest resource version at the time `WatchWriteEvents` is called, so any write that lands between the `ListIterator` snapshot and that call is never replayed into the index. The index can therefore stay permanently stale for those objects. Now that the build runs at startup in the constructor and can take a long time, the window is larger. The watch should be started before the build, with events buffered and applied after the build.

Index build failures now make NewResourceServer fail hard, changing startup behavior

Init is now called synchronously from the constructor, so any error from `search.init` (for example `GetResourceStats` failing, or a bad index build) makes `NewResourceServer` return an error and the whole service fail to start. Previously these errors only surfaced as per-RPC errors and the service stayed up. The `once`/`initErr` mechanism also means the failure is never retried. The PR notes ask exactly this question about what depends on lazy initialization, and the description does not address the startup-failure behavior. Callers in module wiring and tests need to be checked, and the behavior change should be documented or tested.

Unrelated postgres skip added to the storage server integration test

The PR adds a skip for postgres in `TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer`. Nothing in the PR's stated changes (lazy init removal, tracing, locking) relates to postgres. The skip silently removes coverage for the storage-server startup path, which is the path this PR changes, and the TODO gives no tracking issue. Either the test should be fixed or the skip justified in the PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup removes a non-existent IDP named "alias" instead of the created alias

`getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove);` uses the literal string "alias" rather than the alias of the IDP just created. The same mistake appears at line 425 for `idp-alias-20`. The created IDPs are therefore never cleaned up, and they leak into other tests in the class and the shared realm. The cleanup should reference the actual alias (for example via a lambda that captures the alias variable). The same pre-existing pattern in `testCacheIDPByOrg` is copied here.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
getForLogin javadoc omits the new organization public-broker requirement

The javadoc says an IDP is usable for login if it is enabled, not link-only, and not hidden on login. The `getLoginPredicate()` change at line 254 adds a further requirement: an IDP linked to an organization must also have `BROKER_PUBLIC` set to true. The documented contract no longer matches the behaviour, so callers relying on the Javadoc will get wrong expectations about which IDPs are returned.

remove() now always queries the database for the IDP

`IdentityProviderModel storedIdp = idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias);` is now executed unconditionally at the top of `remove()`. Before this change, the DB lookup only happened when the alias cache key was invalidated; the common path used the cached entry. Every removal now incurs an extra uncached DB read, even when the cache already holds the IDP. The lookup should be deferred to the branch that needs it, or the cached model should be reused for the login invalidation check.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead ASN1 encoding computed and discarded in concatenatedRSToASN1DER

Lines 114-115 build two ASN1Encoder instances and throw away the results. The actual return value is computed separately at lines 117-121. The dead calls do unnecessary work and suggest the code was not reviewed carefully.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract method order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

order() is added as an abstract method on a public SPI interface. Any external or test implementation of CryptoProvider that is not updated will fail to compile. Since this is a new capability, a default implementation (for example returning 0 or some documented default) would avoid breaking implementors.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
Oversized integers in DER signatures are silently truncated

integerToBytes() truncates to the last qLength bytes when the BigInteger is longer than the curve size. A malformed or malicious DER signature with an oversized r or s is therefore converted into a different, wrong concatenated signature instead of being rejected. The later verification will fail in a confusing way, or in the worst case the truncated value could be accepted by a verifier. The value should be range-checked and rejected.

Provider is auto-selected for third-party clients but throws for almost every operation

AuthzClient.create() now calls CryptoIntegration.init(), which picks the highest-order provider on the classpath. For a third-party application that only has keycloak-authz-client, AuthzClientCryptoProvider (order 100) becomes the active provider. Most of its methods (getKeyFactory, getKeyPairGen, getSignature, getPemUtils, getCertificateUtils, getIdentityExtractorProvider, getAesGcmCipher, etc.) throw UnsupportedOperationException. Any code path in keycloak-core that calls CryptoIntegration.getProvider() for these, such as parsing PEM keys or RSA keys for client authentication, will fail with a confusing error rather than working. The exposure should be limited, or the unsupported methods should fail clearly and be documented.

Providers with equal order are silently resolved by ServiceLoader order instead of failing

The old code threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. The new code sorts by order() and silently takes the first one. When two providers share the same order, the winner depends on classpath/ServiceLoader iteration order and nothing is reported. Several existing modules declare order 200 (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider), so for example a FIPS build with the default provider also on the classpath would pick an arbitrary one. This silently changes the crypto backend, which is a security-relevant decision. Ties should still be rejected, or resolved by an explicit rule.

Test only checks round-trip consistency, not correctness against the JDK

The test converts a JDK-produced DER signature to concatenated R||S and back, then compares the two concatenated forms. It never checks the output against the JDK's own verifier or a known vector, and it does not test the reverse direction starting from concatenated values with a specific length. A symmetric bug in both directions (for example a wrong byte-padding rule) would still pass. Verifying the signature with the JDK after conversion, and testing leading-zero and short-integer cases, would make the test meaningful.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Role and group removal listeners are now gated behind an unrelated feature flag

The whole listener body was wrapped in an ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ check. Previously the RoleRemovedEvent and GroupRemovedEvent handling ran unconditionally. The PR description says nothing about this change, and it alters cleanup behavior for roles and groups in any realm where the v1 flag is off. Either justify it or keep the original unconditional behavior for the existing branches.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NullPointerException when the 'Clients' resource-type resource is missing

In hasPermission(ClientModel, String), if no per-client resource exists, the code falls back to AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...), which returns null when the resource is absent. The next line then calls policyStore.findByResource(server, null), which will likely NPE. Realms whose resource server was initialized before this PR do not have the new 'Clients' resource, so any client-permission check in those realms can fail with an NPE instead of returning false. Add a null check and return false.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Deleting a client throws UnsupportedOperationException when V2 permissions are enabled

The new ClientRemovedEvent branch calls management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false). When ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is on, management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, whose clients() returns ClientPermissionsV2. ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled (line 193 of that file) unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException. The listener runs on every client removal, so deleting any client in a realm with V2 enabled fails or leaves the deletion half-done. The listener needs a V2-safe path (skip or implement cleanup for V2) before merge.

Existing realms lack the new Clients type and scopes; no migration is provided

init() only creates the Clients resource type and the configure, map-roles-client-scope and map-roles-composite scopes for newly created realms. For realms created before this change, AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource throws 'No scopes found.' when a Clients permission is created, and hasPermission finds no Clients resource at all. No upgrade path or migration is included, so these realms silently get no client permissions or fail on use.

getResourceName does not handle the Clients resource type

getResourceName only special-cases USERS and falls through to resource.getDisplayName() for everything else. Clients resources are created with the internal client UUID as name and no display name, so a client-scope permission lookup may return null or an opaque UUID for display. The Clients type should be mapped to the clientId, analogous to the user username lookup.

requireView() javadoc says it returns a boolean

The javadoc for requireView() reads 'Returns true if canView() returns true', but the method is void and throws ForbiddenException when the check fails. The same wrong wording appears on requireViewClientScopes(). Both should say 'Throws ForbiddenException if ... returns false'.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

false_positives.candidate:
Enabled features are overwritten rather than appended

setEnabledFeatures(List.of(ROLLING_UPDATES)) replaces whatever enabled features the base deployment from getTestKeycloakDeployment already declares. Any feature the shared test base enables is silently dropped for these tests. The list is also immutable, so any later addition to it will throw. Merging with the existing list would be safer.

Null-strategy test variants never enable the rolling-updates feature

createInitialDeployment() returns early when updateStrategy is null, before setFeatureSpec(...) enables ROLLING_UPDATES. The docs in this same PR say the Operator fails when rolling-updates is not enabled. So the testImageChange-null and testCacheMaxCount-null parameterized cases run without the feature and would fail or test the wrong path, unless the base deployment from getTestKeycloakDeployment already enables it. true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() grants group management to holders of only the VIEW scope

In V2, canManage() calls hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE). Because the scope list includes VIEW, any admin with a view-only permission on the Groups type passes canManage(). GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup calls auth.groups().requireManage(), so a view-only admin can create top-level groups. The management check should only accept MANAGE, as canManage(GroupModel) already does.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns resource UUIDs and looks groups up by the wrong key

In V2 each group's Resource is created with name = group id (AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource uses resolveGroup's group id as the name). Lines 121-123 instead add groupResource.getId(), which is the internal resource UUID, not the group id. Line 122 also passes that resource UUID into hasPermission, which calls resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId), so the per-group lookup misses and the code falls back to the all-groups resource. The result is a set of meaningless IDs. Callers use it as a group-ID filter (UserModel.GROUPS and getUsersCount), so users reachable only via a group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permission are never listed or counted. The fix is to use groupResource.getName() for both the lookup and the collected ID.

false_positives.candidate:
Group membership test does not cover the negative case or the view-members path via listing

testManageGroupMembership and testCanViewUserByViewGroupMembers only assert the positive path. No test checks that a user in a group where the admin lacks VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS is hidden, and no test covers the all-groups Groups-type permission combined with a per-group view-members grant. Given the ID bug in getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, the group-membership filter path is the one most likely to regress and is not exercised for V2 from the group-listing side.

Impersonation context uses the target user as the evaluated identity

When a requester is given, canImpersonate builds a DefaultEvaluationContext with new UserModelIdentity(root.realm, user), i.e. the identity being impersonated, not the admin performing the action. Policies attached to the IMPERSONATE permission are then evaluated against the target user's identity. When requester is null, the context is null and evaluation uses the admin's identity. The two paths therefore evaluate different principals, so a policy such as 'only my admin' can allow or deny impersonation depending on whether a client id was passed.

Javadoc for getGroupIdsWithViewPermission describes the wrong return type

The @return tag says 'Stream of IDs of groups with view permission', but the method returns a Set<String>. The sentence before it also reads 'returns empty set', which is correct, but the two statements together are inconsistent with the signature.

NullPointerException when the Groups type resource does not exist

In hasPermission, when the per-group resource is missing, the code loads the all-groups type resource via getResourceTypeResource and immediately calls policyStore.findByResource(server, resource) without a null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null when the resource is absent (e.g. a realm whose schema resources were never initialised), so this throws an NPE instead of returning false. UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission has the same pattern for the Users type.

Public helper searchGroupModelsByAttributes removed from a server SPI module

ModelToRepresentation.searchGroupModelsByAttributes was deleted. It is public in server-spi-private, so any downstream extension or provider code calling it will fail to compile. The only in-repo caller was updated, but the removal is an unannounced API break in a non-test module.

getResourceName has no display name for Groups resources

getResourceName special-cases USERS to show usernames and 'All users', but nothing handles GROUPS. Group permission resources therefore fall back to resource.getDisplayName(), which is typically the raw group UUID. The admin console will show opaque IDs for group permissions, unlike users and clients.

true_positives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Lithuanian translation replaced with Italian text

totpStep1 in messages_lt.properties now reads 'Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:', which is Italian. The Lithuanian user sees untranslated Italian text. The same erroneous Italian string is introduced into login/messages_lt.properties (loginTotpStep1) and must be reverted or properly translated.

true_positives.golden_comment: The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.

The PR says the flusher should spawn a process per redis shard, and SpanFlusher treats a None `max_processes` as one process per assigned shard. But the CLI option defaults to 1, so production consumers that don't pass the flag get a single flusher process for all shards. Restart of a hung thread-based flusher starts a second flusher on the same shards

For threads (the `produce_to_pipe` path), the old thread is left running and `_create_process_for_shards` starts a new thread on the same shards. Two flushers can then concurrently flush the same shard buffer. The previous code would have failed loudly here; now it silently duplicates work. Either refuse to restart threads or make the old one stop before starting the new one.

`_create_process_for_shard` (singular) is never called; restarts go through `_ensure_processes_alive`, which calls `_create_process_for_shards` directly. It is dead code that also duplicates the shard-to-process lookup, so it should be removed or used.

This can happen when `getOrCreateIndex` builds on a Search request while `search.init` is still building the same key, or when a watch event triggers a build. Both paths call `bleve.New` on the same directory for file-backed indexes, and the second call fails. For in-memory indexes, the second build silently replaces the cache entry, leaking the first index and any writes made to it. Nothing in `getOrCreateIndex` or `BuildIndex` deduplicates builds per key, and the TODO in `getOrCreateIndex` acknowledges this. A per-key singleflight or lock is needed before this change is safe.

The candidate adds consequences and mitigation without changing the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

`TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` with no lock, while `BuildIndex` writes to the same map under `cacheMu.Lock()`. The commit removed the whole-function lock and only leaves the map write protected, so this read is now clearly unsynchronized. Concurrent `BuildIndex` calls (for example from `search.init` or a watch-triggered `getOrCreateIndex`) can cause a 'concurrent map read and map write' fatal error. `TotalDocs` should take `cacheMu.RLock()`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same unsynchronized iteration over b.cache in TotalDocs racing with concurrent BuildIndex writes, including watcher-triggered index creation, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Data race on shared `err` and counter in parallel index build goroutines

Inside `init`, each `group.Go` closure runs concurrently and does `totalBatchesIndexed++` (line 189) and `_, _, err = s.build(...)` (line 190). Both `totalBatchesIndexed` and the outer `err` are shared across goroutines, so this is a data race. A failing build can also overwrite another goroutine's error, so `group.Wait()`'s result may not reflect the real failure. The fix is to use a local `err` inside the closure and an atomic counter. This matters more now because the index is built synchronously in the constructor and the locking was made finer, so more builds run concurrently.

Init is now called synchronously from the constructor, so any error from `search.init` (for example `GetResourceStats` failing, or a bad index build) makes `NewResourceServer` return an error and the whole service fail to start. Previously these errors only surfaced as per-RPC errors and the service stayed up. The `once`/`initErr` mechanism also means the failure is never retried. The PR notes ask exactly this question about what depends on lazy initialization, and the description does not address the startup-failure behavior. Callers in module wiring and tests need to be checked, and the behavior change should be documented or tested.

Events written during the index build are never indexed

`init` lists resources and builds the index first, and only afterwards calls `WatchWriteEvents`. The SQL backend's poller starts from the latest resource version at the time `WatchWriteEvents` is called, so any write that lands between the `ListIterator` snapshot and that call is never replayed into the index. The index can therefore stay permanently stale for those objects. Now that the build runs at startup in the constructor and can take a long time, the window is larger. The watch should be started before the build, with events buffered and applied after the build.

Context cancel function is leaked when startup Init fails

`ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` is created earlier in `NewResourceServer`. When `s.Init(ctx)` fails, the function returns `nil, err` without calling `s.cancel()`, and any goroutines started by the lifecycle hook or by `initWatcher`/`search.init` keep running with no owner. The error path should call `cancel()`.

The PR adds a skip for postgres in `TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer`. Nothing in the PR's stated changes (lazy init removal, tracing, locking) relates to postgres. The skip silently removes coverage for the storage-server startup path, which is the path this PR changes, and the TODO gives no tracking issue. Either the test should be fixed or the skip justified in the PR.

false_positives.candidate:
Closing one strategy shuts down the factory's shared queue pool, so later assignments silently drop messages

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` (and `terminate()`/`join()`) call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. The pool is owned by the factory (`ResultsStrategyFactory.queue_pool`) and is reused by every strategy that `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` builds. When StreamProcessor closes a strategy on a rebalance and then calls `create_with_partitions` again, the new strategy gets a pool whose workers have been told to stop and whose queues are shut down. In `submit()` the `put()` on a shut-down queue raises, the broad `except Exception` marks the offset complete via `offset_tracker.add_offset`/`complete_offset`, and the offset is then committed. The message is never processed and never redelivered. The pool should be owned and shut down only by the factory, not by a strategy that merely borrows it.

Offsets are committed from the background commit thread, outside the consumer's processing thread

`_commit_loop` runs on its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which invokes the arroyo `Commit` callable obtained in `create_with_partitions`. Arroyo's consumer and its `Commit` are designed to be driven from the StreamProcessor thread, which also calls `poll()`/`consumer.commit`. Calling commit concurrently from a second thread is not safe for the underlying consumer and can race with rebalance handling and poll. The commit should be marshalled back to the processing thread (for example in `poll()`), or the thread-safety of the consumer path should be explicitly established.

Queues are unbounded, so the claimed backpressure never happens

`FixedQueuePool.__init__` creates `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `submit()` uses a plain `put()`. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`'s docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but nothing ever fills up. If workers are slower than Kafka delivers, the in-memory backlog grows without bound and the consumer never pauses. `poll()` only emits a gauge.

Worker shutdown relies on queue.Queue.shutdown(), which only exists on Python 3.13+

`queue.ShutDown` and `Queue.shutdown()` were added in Python 3.13. On older interpreters `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` raises AttributeError, which is caught and only logged in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()`. Workers stay blocked in `work_queue.get()` forever. `shutdown()` then waits up to 5 seconds per worker (`worker.join(timeout=5.0)`) for up to 20 workers, blocking close for about 100 seconds. The version requirement should be verified, or a sentinel-based shutdown used instead.

Processing failures are logged and then committed, so the message is silently lost

In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, any exception from `result_processor` is logged and the `finally` block marks the offset complete. The commit loop then advances past it, so the failed item is never retried and never reprocessed. The class and module docstrings state 'No item is lost' and 'Only commits offsets after successful processing', which is not what the code does. This should either be documented as at-most-once for failures or the failure should block or retry the commit.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key is ambiguous because fields are joined with '_' and names can contain '_'

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates name and parent with '_' separators without escaping. Different tuples produce the same key, e.g. name="a_", parent="b" and name="a", parent="_b" both yield "...action_a__b". A denial recorded for one resource then short-circuits Check for another resource with a colliding key, returning a wrong deny. Dashboard and folder UIDs can contain underscores, so this can happen. Use an unambiguous encoding (length prefix, or a separator that cannot appear in UIDs).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify ambiguous underscore-based concatenation in userPermDenialCacheKey, allowing different component tuples to collide and cause incorrect permission denial cache hits. The candidate provides a concrete example of the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Permission denials are cached for 30s with no invalidation, so a newly granted permission stays denied

When the DB check returns not-allowed, the result is stored in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL (30s), keyed by user, action, name and parent folder. Nothing invalidates this entry when permissions change. The PR's stated goal is that a creator can access a dashboard or folder they just created. If the user is first denied on that name (for example a fetch before creation), the denial is then served from cache for up to 30s even though the DB now grants access. The denial cache check at line 116-121 returns before the DB fallback runs, so the new-permission fallback never applies during that window. Either skip caching denials, use a much shorter TTL, or invalidate the entry when a permission or resource is created.

Folder tree stays cached for 30s after folder creation, so inherited access to new nested folders is denied

buildFolderTree caches the namespace folder tree for shortCacheTTL and nothing invalidates it on folder creation. The fallback to the DB only refreshes permissions, not the folder tree. For a folder created within the TTL, e.g. grandchild C under a newly created child B under a folder A the user already has access to, the tree lacks C (and possibly B). checkInheritedPermissions then calls tree.Ancestors(C), which cannot reach A, so the creator is denied on a dashboard in C even though they hold a grant on A. This is the same user-facing bug the PR aims to fix, and it is not covered by the new fallback. Refresh the folder tree on a miss for the requested folder, or invalidate it on folder creation.

New cache tests do not cover the behaviour the PR is meant to fix

TestService_CacheCheck covers cache hits, DB fallback on a miss or outdated map, and a pre-set explicit denial. It never checks that a DB denial populates the denial cache, nor that a permission granted after a denial is honoured (the creator scenario). It also has no test for inherited access through a folder created after the tree was cached, and no test for denial key collisions. These are the scenarios that would catch the staleness and key issues above.

This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Write lock taken without re-checking the cache, and held across file and CDN I/O

The fast path reads the cache under RLock, releases it, then takes the write lock at line 48 without checking the cache again. Every goroutine that misses the cache during startup, or after a failed load, will queue on the write lock and each one re-runs the manifest read and, when configured, the HTTP fetch to the CDN. The lock is held for the whole rebuild (lines 48-70), including the network call in readWebAssetsFromCDN, which has no timeout beyond the request context. Before this change, readers never blocked. Now every request that reaches GetWebAssets blocks on the write lock for as long as a slow CDN takes to respond. Fix: after acquiring the write lock, re-read entryPointAssetsCache and return it if it is now non-nil and not in Dev mode. Consider doing the I/O outside the lock and taking the lock only to publish the result.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the missing cache re-check after acquiring the write lock, which is the same incomplete double-checked locking issue described by the golden comment. The additional concern about holding the lock during I/O does not negate the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error path caches nil and returns a stale-looking result

On error, result is nil and line 69 overwrites the global cache with nil, so the cache is cleared even if a previous good value existed (for example, in Dev mode where the cache is reloaded on every call). The function then returns nil with err. Callers that ignore err will get a nil pointer. This behaviour is unchanged by the diff, but the new locking makes it more visible: a transient read failure during a Dev reload now clears the shared cache for concurrent readers. Consider only assigning the cache when err == nil.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same error-handling bug: assigning a nil fetch result to entryPointAssetsCache on failure overwrites a previously valid cached value. The candidate also recommends assigning the cache only when err == nil.

false_positives.candidate:

The PR fixes a data race on entryPointAssetsCache, but no test is added or changed. A test that calls GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines, ideally under go test -race and covering both Dev and non-Dev environments, would show the race is fixed and would catch the locking regression described above.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes run on the request context, so they are cancelled once the request returns

Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection launch the legacy write in a goroutine using a context derived from the request ctx (e.g. line 51 `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). The HTTP request context is cancelled when the handler returns, which happens right after the storage write succeeds. The legacy write will therefore often fail with context canceled, and the failure is only recorded in metrics. Legacy writes can silently be skipped, which defeats the purpose of mode 3's safety copy. The goroutine should use a detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx)) plus the timeout.

Object passed to the async legacy Create is shared with the storage Create and may be mutated concurrently

The same `obj` is handed to d.Storage.Create (line 42) and then to d.Legacy.Create inside a goroutine (line 55). Storage create implementations typically mutate the object (set ResourceVersion, UID, creationTimestamp, name generation). The legacy goroutine therefore reads an object that may be written concurrently or is already modified, which is a data race and can write inconsistent data to legacy. The legacy path should get a DeepCopy taken before the goroutine starts, or the storage result should be used.

Async legacy Update reuses objInfo that the storage Update has already consumed

objInfo is passed to d.Storage.Update (line 126) and then reused in the legacy goroutine (line 139). UpdatedObjectInfo.UpdatedObject is typically called once per store and may consume or mutate the old object; calling it concurrently from the goroutine races with the storage path. Also the legacy update may compute its update from a different base object than the one storage used, so the two stores can diverge without any error being surfaced.

Storage Update failure is recorded as a legacy duration metric

In the Update error path, the failure is recorded with d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) and startStorage, even though the failing call was the storage write. This corrupts legacy metrics and hides storage failures from the storage metric.

Legacy DeleteCollection duration and errors are recorded as storage metrics

In the goroutine, the legacy DeleteCollection result is recorded via d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...) (line 166) instead of recordLegacyDuration. Legacy failures are counted as storage and legacy metrics stay empty for this method.

Legacy write failures in async goroutines are not logged

Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection run the legacy write in a goroutine and only record a metric on error. There is no log call, so a failed legacy write leaves no trace in logs and divergence between the stores is invisible to operators. The old code logged these failures, so this is a regression in observability.

Update goroutine creates its timeout context before startLegacy and without a defer on the same line

In the Update goroutine (lines 135-138) the timeout context is created before the timer starts and the cancel is deferred after an unrelated statement. This is harmless today but is inconsistent with the other goroutines and makes the cancel easy to miss if the function is edited. Low priority.

Error test for Create passes only because the legacy expectation matches the storage call

The 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' case registers no storage expectation (setupStorageFn is nil). The storage Create call therefore matches the legacy mock expectation at line 41 and returns the error by accident. The test does not check what it claims to check, and a change in the call pattern would make it panic instead of asserting.

Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy write or wait for it

The tests set legacy mock expectations but never assert they were called (AssertExpectations is not used), and the goroutines are not awaited. Tests pass even when legacy is never written, and goroutines can call mocks after the test has finished. The behavior that defines mode 3 (legacy write happens and does not fail the request) is not tested.

Get test creates its own registry while the other tests share the package-level registry

TestMode3_Get creates a new prometheus registry (line 119) while all other tests, and the mode1 test after this change, use the shared package-level `p`. Mixing the two patterns is inconsistent and makes it unclear whether the dual writer metrics are registered more than once on the shared registry across subtests.

Mode 3 playlist integration tests check legacy consistency immediately after writes that are now asynchronous

doPlaylistTests asserts legacy API results right after k8s creates, updates and deletes (for example the legacy list check after Create, and getFromBothAPIs after Update). With mode 3 the legacy write runs in a background goroutine, so these checks can race with it and fail intermittently. The new mode 3 subtests need a wait or retry before comparing the legacy store, or the assertions must be relaxed for mode 3.

Unrelated module checksum entries added to go.work.sum

The go.work.sum diff adds checksums for unrelated modules (grafana-azure-sdk-go/v2, prometheus-alertmanager, otel exporters, genproto rpc, etc.) that have nothing to do with the dual writer change. These look like incidental tooling output and should be removed from this PR to keep the change focused.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.

CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices (line 110) and then separately inserts or updates (lines 115-118 and below). Concurrent first-time requests from distinct devices can all read a count below the limit and all insert, so the number of devices can exceed deviceLimit. A correct enforcement needs a single atomic statement or a transaction/lock, and the race should be acknowledged or tested if it is not fixed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: concurrent requests can pass a non-atomic device count check and insert devices beyond the limit. Both suggest atomic enforcement through a transaction or lock.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
rowsAffected == 0 is treated as limit reached, which misfires on MySQL

updateDevice treats zero affected rows as ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL, the default driver behaviour reports only changed rows, so an UPDATE that rewrites identical client_ip and user_agent values (common for a returning device) reports 0 rows and is wrongly rejected as if the limit were reached. Also, a device whose updated_at is older than the 30-day window matches nothing and is rejected, even though it already exists and should be updated. The error conflates 'row not found in window' with 'limit reached'.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the incorrect mapping of zero affected rows in updateDevice to ErrDeviceLimitReached. The candidate explicitly covers devices outside the time window and the conflation of no matching row with a reached limit, matching the golden issue despite adding a MySQL-specific scenario.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.

Device is cached before the limit check, so a rejected device is later let in

tagDeviceUI stores the device key in localCache (line 87) before CreateOrUpdateDevice runs. When the limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached and the device is not tagged, but the key stays cached. For the next ~29 minutes, every request from that device hits the cache hit at line 83 and returns nil, so Authenticate succeeds without the device ever being counted. The first rejection is effectively followed by a bypass of the limit. The cache key should only be set after a successful tag, or removed on error.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: tagDeviceUI caches the device before CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds, leaving the entry cached after ErrDeviceLimitReached and allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit for approximately 29 minutes.

false_positives.candidate:
Device tagging is now synchronous on every anonymous authentication

For any device not in the local cache, each request performs a COUNT over the 30-day window and then a write, so database latency is added directly to every anonymous page load and API call. Slow or contended DB writes now slow or block authentication, and the panic recovery that the goroutine had is also gone.

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only covers a new device being rejected. It does not check that an already-registered device under the limit is still updated when the limit is reached, that a device outside the 30-day window is handled, or that re-tagging with unchanged values succeeds on MySQL. false_positives.candidate:
Translation cache key ignores the site default locale that now drives fallbacks

The LRU cache key is built from the key, `config.locale` and the backend object_id only. With this PR, the result of `translate` also depends on `SiteSetting.default_locale`, because `FallbackLocaleList#[]` inserts that locale into the fallback chain. After the site default locale changes, cached entries for user locales that fell back to the old default (or to :en) keep being served until they are evicted or `reload!` runs. The key should include the fallback chain or the default locale.

Fallback chain is rebuilt and reads SiteSetting on every lookup and every request

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` allocates a new array and calls `SiteSetting.default_locale` on each call. `set_locale` in ApplicationController calls `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` on every request, which invokes `self[I18n.locale]` and so repeats that work. The Fallbacks backend also calls `I18n.fallbacks[locale]` for every missing-key translation. This is small per call but runs on the hot path.

ensure_loaded! only loads the chain for the current locale, not for an explicitly passed locale

`ensure_loaded!` loads only `self[I18n.locale]`. Lookups made with an explicit `locale:` argument, or from background jobs that switch locale without going through `set_locale`, will use a fallback chain whose translation files may not be loaded yet. The lazy `load_locale` in the accelerator only covers `config.locale`, so the fallback locales can be missing without any error.

Pull request description is a placeholder

The PR description reads only 'Test 9'. It gives no explanation of why fallbacks move from environment configs into an initializer, why `pluralization.rb` is merged into `i18n.rb`, or how the fallback chain is meant to behave. Reviewers cannot check the intent of the change from the PR itself.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).
