false_positives.candidate:
Stored hosts are not normalized to lowercase, so mixed-case hosts never match

The validation regex is case-insensitive (`/i`), so `Example.com` is accepted and stored as-is. `record_for_host` compares `lower(host) = ?` against the lowercased referer/URL host, but the stored value is not lowercased. A host saved with uppercase letters therefore never matches, and embeds from that domain are rejected or import into the wrong category. Lowercase the host in before_validation, or compare with `lower(host) = lower(?)`.

No uniqueness validation on host, so duplicate entries are allowed

Nothing prevents the same host from being created twice. `record_for_host` uses `.first` with no ordering, so which category a host maps to becomes arbitrary when duplicates exist. The embedding admin list would also show duplicate rows. Add a uniqueness validation (case-insensitive) and ideally a unique index.

create_table with force: true silently drops an existing table

If embeddable_hosts already exists (for example on a partial or re-run migration, or a table created by another branch), `force: true` drops it along with any data in it. Dropping this table is unnecessary for a fresh migration and risks data loss. Remove `force: true`.

Missing embeddable_host param raises NoMethodError

`params[:embeddable_host][:host]` is accessed without checking that the `embeddable_host` key exists, so a request without it causes a 500 rather than a validation error.

update action accepts changes but never saves anything

`update` only re-renders the serialized embedding. Nothing is persisted, so a PUT to /admin/customize/embedding reports success while discarding its input. The client `saveChanges` action calls this endpoint and therefore appears to save while doing nothing. Either implement the save or remove the route and client call.

saveChanges sends an empty update that does nothing

`this.get('embedding').update({})` sends an empty payload to the server, which ignores it. This is dead or misleading code, since host changes are saved per row by the component.

Spec only checks class inheritance; create/update/destroy are untested

The only test asserts that the controller subclasses AdminController. The actual behavior (creating, updating, destroying hosts, the uncategorized default for blank category, and the not-found and invalid-input paths) has no test coverage.

Embedding controller spec has no behavior tests

The spec only checks inheritance. The show and update endpoints, and the staff-only access check, are not exercised.

Topic is created with nil category when no host record matches

The category now comes only from EmbeddableHost. If no host record matches (for example because of the case-sensitivity issue above, or a host that was deleted), `category` becomes nil. The previous behavior of falling back to a configured category is gone, and nothing falls back to the uncategorized category.

false_negatives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.

Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.

It runs on every validation pass, not only when a user is actually refused. `valid?` followed by `save`, retries, or any extra validation call will count one blocked attempt several times, so the statistics become unreliable. Read-only checking should be separate from recording a block.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying issue: a method that checks whether an email is blocked also mutates match statistics. The candidate emphasizes repeated validation inflating counts, while the golden emphasizes race conditions and misleading naming, but both concern side effects in a read-only check.

The PR is about flexbox layout, so these visual changes look unintended and are not covered by the description.

Under the new flex container, floats on flex items are ignored anyway, so the only way the element keeps its position is through the flex order. `.small-action` becomes a flex container, but its children still rely on floats: `.topic-avatar { float: left }`, `.small-action-desc .avatar { float: left }`, and `button { float: right }`. false_positives.candidate:
RSS/Atom item HTML is unescaped and stored as raw, unsanitized post HTML

`CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` turns the feed's escaped markup back into real HTML, and `TopicEmbed.import` then stores it with `cook_method: raw_html`. `Post#cook` returns `raw` unchanged for raw_html posts, so the content skips the sanitizing pipeline and is rendered as-is by `best.html.erb` (`raw post.cooked`). A feed item containing `<script>` or event-handler attributes becomes stored XSS in the embedding page's iframe and the forum.

Failed post creation is not detected before creating the TopicEmbed row

`PostCreator#create` returns `@post` even when validation or spam checks fail (the post is unsaved, with errors). `if post.present?` is true in that case, so `TopicEmbed.create!` runs with `post.topic_id` possibly nil. This raises a NOT NULL database error or a validation error inside the background job, rather than cleanly returning nil. The check should be `post.present? && post.persisted?`.

Each unknown embed URL triggers a synchronous full feed download

`perform_retrieve` calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` whenever RSS polling is enabled and the URL is not yet known. That downloads and parses the entire feed and re-imports every item, with no timeout and no caching. Every distinct new URL repeats this work, so a burst of embed requests means many full feed fetches.

Removing the function-wide lock means two `BuildIndex` calls for the same NamespacedResource can run at once. This can happen when `getOrCreateIndex` builds on a Search request while `search.init` is still building the same key, or when a watch event triggers a build. Both paths call `bleve.New` on the same directory for file-backed indexes, and the second call fails. For in-memory indexes, the second build silently replaces the cache entry, leaking the first index and any writes made to it. Nothing in `getOrCreateIndex` or `BuildIndex` deduplicates builds per key, and the TODO in `getOrCreateIndex` acknowledges this. A per-key singleflight or lock is needed before this change is safe.

`TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` with no lock, while `BuildIndex` writes to the same map under `cacheMu.Lock()`. The commit removed the whole-function lock and only leaves the map write protected, so this read is now clearly unsynchronized. Concurrent `BuildIndex` calls (for example from `search.init` or a watch-triggered `getOrCreateIndex`) can cause a 'concurrent map read and map write' fatal error. `TotalDocs` should take `cacheMu.RLock()`.

false_positives.candidate:
Data race on shared `err` and counter in parallel index build goroutines

Inside `init`, each `group.Go` closure runs concurrently and does `totalBatchesIndexed++` (line 189) and `_, _, err = s.build(...)` (line 190). Both `totalBatchesIndexed` and the outer `err` are shared across goroutines, so this is a data race. A failing build can also overwrite another goroutine's error, so `group.Wait()`'s result may not reflect the real failure. The fix is to use a local `err` inside the closure and an atomic counter. This matters more now because the index is built synchronously in the constructor and the locking was made finer, so more builds run concurrently.

Index build failures now make NewResourceServer fail hard, changing startup behavior

Init is now called synchronously from the constructor, so any error from `search.init` (for example `GetResourceStats` failing, or a bad index build) makes `NewResourceServer` return an error and the whole service fail to start. Previously these errors only surfaced as per-RPC errors and the service stayed up. The `once`/`initErr` mechanism also means the failure is never retried. The PR notes ask exactly this question about what depends on lazy initialization, and the description does not address the startup-failure behavior. Callers in module wiring and tests need to be checked, and the behavior change should be documented or tested.

Events written during the index build are never indexed

`init` lists resources and builds the index first, and only afterwards calls `WatchWriteEvents`. The SQL backend's poller starts from the latest resource version at the time `WatchWriteEvents` is called, so any write that lands between the `ListIterator` snapshot and that call is never replayed into the index. The index can therefore stay permanently stale for those objects. Now that the build runs at startup in the constructor and can take a long time, the window is larger. The watch should be started before the build, with events buffered and applied after the build.

Context cancel function is leaked when startup Init fails

`ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` is created earlier in `NewResourceServer`. When `s.Init(ctx)` fails, the function returns `nil, err` without calling `s.cancel()`, and any goroutines started by the lifecycle hook or by `initWatcher`/`search.init` keep running with no owner. The error path should call `cancel()`.

The skip silently removes coverage for the storage-server startup path, which is the path this PR changes, and the TODO gives no tracking issue. Either the test should be fixed or the skip justified in the PR.

Closing one strategy shuts down the factory's shared queue pool, so later assignments silently drop messages

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` (and `terminate()`/`join()`) call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. When StreamProcessor closes a strategy on a rebalance and then calls `create_with_partitions` again, the new strategy gets a pool whose workers have been told to stop and whose queues are shut down. In `submit()` the `put()` on a shut-down queue raises, the broad `except Exception` marks the offset complete via `offset_tracker.add_offset`/`complete_offset`, and the offset is then committed. The message is never processed and never redelivered. The pool should be owned and shut down only by the factory, not by a strategy that merely borrows it.

Offsets are committed from the background commit thread, outside the consumer's processing thread

`_commit_loop` runs on its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which invokes the arroyo `Commit` callable obtained in `create_with_partitions`. Arroyo's consumer and its `Commit` are designed to be driven from the StreamProcessor thread, which also calls `poll()`/`consumer.commit`. Calling commit concurrently from a second thread is not safe for the underlying consumer and can race with rebalance handling and poll. The commit should be marshalled back to the processing thread (for example in `poll()`), or the thread-safety of the consumer path should be explicitly established.

Queues are unbounded, so the claimed backpressure never happens

`FixedQueuePool.__init__` creates `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `submit()` uses a plain `put()`. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`'s docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but nothing ever fills up. If workers are slower than Kafka delivers, the in-memory backlog grows without bound and the consumer never pauses. `poll()` only emits a gauge.

Worker shutdown relies on queue.Queue.shutdown(), which only exists on Python 3.13+

`queue.ShutDown` and `Queue.shutdown()` were added in Python 3.13. On older interpreters `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` raises AttributeError, which is caught and only logged in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()`. Workers stay blocked in `work_queue.get()` forever. `shutdown()` then waits up to 5 seconds per worker (`worker.join(timeout=5.0)`) for up to 20 workers, blocking close for about 100 seconds. The version requirement should be verified, or a sentinel-based shutdown used instead.

Processing failures are logged and then committed, so the message is silently lost

The class and module docstrings state 'No item is lost' and 'Only commits offsets after successful processing', which is not what the code does. `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` turns the feed's escaped markup back into real HTML, and `TopicEmbed.import` then stores it with `cook_method: raw_html`. `Post#cook` returns `raw` unchanged for raw_html posts, so the content skips the sanitizing pipeline and is rendered as-is by `best.html.erb` (`raw post.cooked`). `PostCreator#create` returns `@post` even when validation or spam checks fail (the post is unsaved, with errors). `if post.present?` is true in that case, so `TopicEmbed.create!` runs with `post.topic_id` possibly nil. This raises a NOT NULL database error or a validation error inside the background job, rather than cleanly returning nil. The check should be `post.present? && post.persisted?`.

Each unknown embed URL triggers a synchronous full feed download

`perform_retrieve` calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` whenever RSS polling is enabled and the URL is not yet known. That downloads and parses the entire feed and re-imports every item, with no timeout and no caching. Every distinct new URL repeats this work, so a burst of embed requests means many full feed fetches.

For any unknown `embed_url`, `best` enqueues a `retrieve_topic` job. The 60-second throttle in `TopicRetriever` is keyed by the exact URL string, so each distinct query string or path on the embeddable host bypasses it. Anonymous clients can generate arbitrarily many fetch-and-create jobs against the forum and the embeddable site.

If the process dies between `$redis.setnx` and `$redis.expire`, the `retrieved:` key is left with no TTL. That URL is then throttled permanently. Use `SET key 1 EX 60 NX` or an equivalent single command.

`TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` followed by a create is not safe under concurrency. Two jobs importing the same URL can both see no embed, and the second insert violates the unique index on `embed_url`, raising an exception after a duplicate topic and post have already been created in the transaction.

`t.string :embed_url, null: false` uses the default 255-character limit. Article URLs with long query strings or paths exceed this and fail on insert in PostgreSQL. Since the value is also the unique key, a longer text column or an explicit limit with validation is needed.

`message` is a template string that always contains the separator, so `message || t("unable_to_add_guests")` never falls back. The intended fallback is never shown on errors with no code.

The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code single-use is not enforced atomically

The backup code is consumed by reading the encrypted list, setting the matched entry to null in memory, and writing the whole list back with a plain update. Nothing ties the write to the value that was read. Two concurrent login requests that present the same valid code (both pass the password check and read the same list) will both succeed, and the second write will simply overwrite the first. A code documented as 'can be used exactly once' can therefore be redeemed more than once. A conditional update (compare-and-swap on the stored ciphertext, or a transaction with a re-check) is needed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same non-atomic backup-code consumption: concurrent requests can read the same code, pass validation, and overwrite each other's update, allowing one-time reuse.

false_positives.candidate:
missing_backup_codes message points to a settings option that does not exist

The message tells users 'No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings.' No regenerate or view-codes UI is added by this PR. Codes are only created during the initial 2FA setup, and disabling 2FA is required to get new ones. Users who see this message are sent to a place where they cannot act on it, so the text is misleading.

Backup codes are unrecoverable if the dialog is dismissed without clicking Close

Backup codes are shown only in the DisplayBackupCodes step, and the dialog's own close control (onOpenChange / Escape / overlay click) bypasses the 'backup-codes-close' button. The codes are stored hashed-to-nothing (encrypted only, and never shown again). Once the user dismisses the dialog, the codes can no longer be retrieved, and the only way to get new ones is to disable and re-enable 2FA. Nothing in the flow forces the user to acknowledge or save the codes before dismissal.

Copy button reports success even if the clipboard write fails

navigator.clipboard.writeText(...) is not awaited or caught, and the success toast is shown unconditionally. The Clipboard API rejects in insecure contexts or when permission is denied, so the user gets a 'Backup codes copied!' toast while nothing was copied, and an unhandled promise rejection is produced.

Interactive Button rendered inside an anchor element

The download control nests a <Button> (a <button> element) inside an <a download> element. Interactive content inside <a> is invalid HTML, has inconsistent keyboard and click behaviour across browsers, and is an accessibility problem. The anchor should carry the styling or the button should be the link.

Password visibility toggle removed from keyboard tab order for all PasswordField uses

tabIndex={-1} is added to the show/hide password button inside the shared PasswordField component. This affects every password field in the app, not only the 2FA flow, and makes the toggle unreachable by keyboard users. The change is unrelated to backup codes and is an accessibility regression.

Non-string backupCode in request body causes an unhandled exception

req.body.backupCode.replaceAll(...) assumes a string. A client sending a number, object, or array as backupCode (the body is unvalidated JSON) throws a TypeError, which surfaces as a 500 rather than a 400 IncorrectBackupCode. The same pattern exists in next-auth-options.ts for credentials.backupCode.

Backup-code login path has no test coverage

The new login flow (Lost access, backup code submission, incorrect and missing backup code errors, and single-use consumption) is not exercised by any test. The only backup-code assertions are that the download, copy, and close buttons exist in the setup dialog. The PR description says the feature is untested, and the TODO only defers this. The core behaviour of the feature, including the single-use guarantee, is unverified.

Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

`calendarId = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` only matches when externalCalendarId is truthy, but in the fallback branch it is falsy, so the lookup always returns undefined. true_positives.golden_comment: The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

createEvent (and createAttendees/updateEvent/deleteEvent) derive the calendar id from `event.destinationCalendar[0]` only. Since EventManager now calls createEvent once per destination (passing `destination.externalId`), every Lark credential creates its event on the first host's calendar. For collective events with multiple hosts, the second host's Lark event is created in the wrong calendar and duplicates are placed on the first host's calendar. The explicit externalId/credential is never used.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.

createEvent always uses `event.destinationCalendar[0]` for the target calendar. With multiple destinations (collective event), EventManager invokes createEvent for each host credential, but the Office365 service ignores which credential it belongs to and writes every host's event into the first host's calendar. The PR's goal of inviting each host correctly is not met for Outlook.

Recurring cancellation deletes events once per calendar reference

The bookingCalendarReference loop now iterates every calendar reference. Inside, the recurring branch (`allRemainingBookings`) re-runs the whole loop over all user calendar credentials and all updatedBookings, so with N calendar references each remaining booking's event is deleted N times. Duplicate deleteEvent calls push duplicate promises into apiDeletes and can produce spurious errors. The recurring deletion should run once outside the per-reference loop.

Dynamic-user query drops organization select and adds broad error mapping

In the loadUsers rewrite, the `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` clause was removed from the dynamic user findMany. Downstream code that relies on organization slug for dynamic group bookings will now get undefined. The new try/catch also converts every non-HttpError/non-Prisma error into a generic 500 'Unable to load users', hiding the real cause, and treats an empty dynamicUserList as a 400 that previously could have been handled differently.

Collective co-host destination calendars dropped when organizer has none

Team destination calendars are appended with `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...)`. If the organizer has no destinationCalendar, `evt.destinationCalendar` is `null` and the push is silently skipped, so the other collective hosts' calendars are never added, which is the exact case this PR is meant to fix. The array should be initialized before pushing.

PR ships no tests for multi-destination behavior

The PR changes the destinationCalendar contract across ~20 files (array shape, per-credential selection, fallbacks) but adds no unit or e2e tests. The checklist explicitly says tests were not added. The collective multi-host scenario and the array-to-single fallbacks are untested, which is how the regressions above slipped through.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Making the forEach callback async moves getCalendar errors out of the try/catch

Before this change, `getCalendar` was synchronous, so a throw inside it was caught by the surrounding try/catch and logged. Now the callback is async and the `await getCalendar(...)` and `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` promises are not awaited by `forEach`, so rejections become unhandled promise rejections and the try/catch never sees them. The cancellation work also runs fire-and-forget, so the reschedule returns before calendar/video deletion finishes. The same pattern is in packages/app-store/wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same core bug: async callbacks passed to forEach are not awaited, so calendar/video deletion promises escape the surrounding try/catch, become unhandled rejections, and run fire-and-forget. The narrower file reference does not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
import() calls run eagerly at module load, so nothing is actually lazy

Each entry is `import("./x")` evaluated when the object literal is created, so every app module starts loading as soon as `appStore` is imported, regardless of whether it is used. The async wrapping therefore adds no lazy-loading benefit on the server or in client bundles. Entries should be thunks (`() => import("./x")`) and callers should invoke them on demand. Any rejected import is also created up front, so a broken app module can surface as an unhandled rejection even if nothing ever awaits it.

requestReschedule fires async calendar/video deletions without awaiting them

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...)` discards the promises returned by each callback. The mutation then sends the reschedule email and returns while the `getCalendar` lookup and the `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` calls are still running. Any rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection, and the client cannot know whether the old calendar event was actually removed. Use `Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` and await it.

Async forEach pushes into apiDeletes after it has already been awaited

Inside the recurring-cancellation branch, `.forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })` pushes to `apiDeletes` only after an asynchronous await. `forEach` does not wait for these callbacks, so `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` runs before the pushes happen. Those deletions are never awaited, their errors are unhandled, and the response can report success while calendar events are still being deleted. Replace the forEach with a for...of loop or `Promise.all` over the credentials.

Adapter creation is now sequential and awaits each app in a loop

`getVideoAdapters` used to build adapters synchronously in one pass. It now awaits each app import one at a time in a `for` loop, so N credentials cost N sequential module-load round trips. Resolving the apps with `Promise.all` would preserve ordering and avoid the serialized waits.

getCalendarCredentials stores un-awaited getCalendar promises as the calendar value

`getCalendarCredentials` is still synchronous, but `getCalendar` now returns a Promise, so `calendar` is a Promise on every returned item. Any consumer that checks `if (!calendar)` or uses the value as a Calendar synchronously will be wrong. A rejected `getCalendar` promise (for example from a failing CalendarService constructor) is also only handled when `getConnectedCalendars` later awaits it, so the rejection can be reported late or unhandled. The function should be made async and should await the calendar, or the field type should be updated to match.
